meta.titre: Business Cycles: phases, causes and stabilisation
meta.sous_theme: Phases of the trade cycle and the accelerator

sections.contenu_markdown: When the world price of cocoa or coffee rises, farmers and traders across Cameroon spend more, shops are busy and firms hire. When prices fall, incomes shrink, orders drop and some firms close. Economies do not grow at an even pace; they alternate between faster and slower growth, and these swings are called business cycles. Examiners ask you to name the phases, describe them, explain what causes the swings and judge what governments can do. This course gives you all four skills.

items: Real national output (real GDP) is the value of goods and services produced in a country, adjusted for price changes.
Investment is spending on capital goods; consumption is spending on goods and services by households.
A rise in autonomous spending raises national income by a multiple of itself, which is the multiplier effect.
Unemployment is the situation of people who are able and willing to work but have no job.

sections.titre: The business cycle: four phases and their features
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Definition
The **business cycle** (or **trade cycle**) is the tendency of real national output to fluctuate around its long-term trend, with periods of fast growth followed by slow growth or falling output. Cycles vary in length and size, so they are **irregular, not regular and predictable**.

### The four phases
| Phase | Output and employment | Prices and profits | Investment and confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Boom** (peak) | Output high and near full capacity; unemployment low | Rising prices, risk of inflation, high profits | High investment, high confidence; shortages of labour and materials |
| **Recession** (downswing) | Growth slows and then output falls; unemployment rises | Demand falls, profits fall, price rises slow down | Investment is cut, confidence falls, stocks of unsold goods build up |
| **Depression** (slump, trough) | Output very low, high unemployment, spare capacity | Prices stagnant or falling, many firms fail | Gross investment very low, interest rates low; late in the slump worn-out machines must be replaced, so replacement investment begins |
| **Recovery** (upswing) | Output and employment begin to rise | Profits begin to improve | Confidence returns, investment and consumer spending rise, and the multiplier spreads the rise |

A common definition of a recession is **two consecutive quarters of falling real output**. Books use different names (expansion, contraction, trough), so learn the alternatives.

### Why the turning points happen
At the **peak**, shortages of resources and rising costs and interest rates slow the boom. At the **trough**, worn-out capital has to be replaced, so **replacement investment begins** late in the slump and marks the turning point to recovery. Rising confidence and expansionary policy help, and the multiplier then amplifies the rise. Textbooks place this point at the end of the depression or the start of recovery, so describe it as the turning point. Note that the **peak is the highest level of output**, not the highest growth rate: output keeps rising while growth slows.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions that ask why output fluctuates
variantes.contenu_markdown:
- **Fluctuations in investment:** investment depends on expectations, so it is volatile, and the multiplier magnifies its changes.
- **The accelerator:** net investment depends on the change in output: $I_{net} = v \times \Delta Y$, where $v$ is the capital-output ratio. If output grows more slowly, investment can fall even though output is still rising, which can start a downswing.
- **Confidence and expectations:** waves of optimism and pessimism (what Keynes called animal spirits) can reinforce booms and slumps.
- **Credit and interest rates:** easy credit fuels booms; tight credit and high interest rates slow them.
- **External shocks:** changes in world prices of exports such as cocoa, oil price shocks, poor harvests or wars.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions on how to reduce the effects of the cycle
variantes.contenu_markdown: In a slump the government can use **expansionary** policy: higher government spending, lower taxes and lower interest rates, to raise aggregate demand and reduce unemployment. In a boom it can use **contractionary** policy: lower spending, higher taxes and higher interest rates, to avoid inflation. Evaluation: it is hard to identify the phase of the cycle at the time; policies take time to work and may act when the cycle has already turned; higher spending may increase the budget deficit; and external shocks are outside the government's control.

Booms bring jobs and rising incomes but also inflation, shortages and a larger deficit in trade. Slumps bring unemployment, lost output, falling profits, business failures and falling tax revenue. Large swings make planning and investment harder, so many governments try to smooth them.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The table shows the annual percentage change in real national output of an imaginary economy. Output at the start of year 1 is taken as 100.

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Change in output (%) | +5 | +6 | +1 | -2 | -3 | 0 | +3 | +5 |

(a) Calculate the index of output at the end of each year.
(b) Identify the year of the peak and the phases of the cycle.
(c) Explain why year 3 is not a recession although growth slows.
(d) State two features expected in year 5.

etapes.justification: Each year's output is the previous level multiplied by (1 + the growth rate).
The peak is the year when the level of output is highest before it falls.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Output rises until year 3 (112.4) and then falls, so the **peak is in year 3**.

etapes.justification: Phases follow the direction and level of output.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Years 1 to 3: expansion up to the boom. Years 4 and 5: recession (output falls). End of year 5 and year 6: trough, with output at its lowest and not growing. Years 7 and 8: recovery.

etapes.action: Explain why year 3 is not a recession.
etapes.justification: A recession is a fall in output, not a slower rate of growth.
etapes.resultat_markdown: In year 3 output still rises by 1 per cent, from 111.3 to 112.4. Growth slowed, which warns of the downturn, but output did not fall.

etapes.justification: Features come from the table of phases.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Output falls again, unemployment is rising or high, profits and investment are weak, and confidence is low.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) The index reads 105.0, 111.3, 112.4, 110.2, 106.9, 106.9, 110.1 and 115.6. (b) The peak is in year 3; years 4 and 5 are recession, years 5 to 6 are the trough and years 7 and 8 are recovery. (c) Year 3 is not a recession because output still rises, only more slowly. (d) In year 5 unemployment is high or rising and investment and profits are low.

items.erreur_markdown: Confusing a fall in the growth rate with a fall in output.
items.pourquoi_faux: A recession is a fall in the level of real output. Output can keep rising while the growth rate falls.
items.correction_markdown: Write that a recession needs falling output, and that a slowdown in growth is only an early warning.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing a depression with rising prices and high investment.
items.pourquoi_faux: In a slump demand is weak, so prices are stagnant or falling, and investment is very low.
items.correction_markdown: Link each phase to its features: low output, high unemployment, weak demand and low investment in the slump.

items.erreur_markdown: "Business cycles are regular and last the same number of years."
items.pourquoi_faux: Cycles differ in length and size, and their turning points are hard to predict.
items.correction_markdown: Say that cycles are recurrent but irregular.

items.erreur_markdown: Listing the four phases without any explanation.
items.pourquoi_faux: A list gains few marks. The command word asks for description or explanation.
items.correction_markdown: Describe the output, employment, prices and investment of each phase and explain how one phase leads to the next.

items.erreur_markdown: "A boom has no disadvantages because unemployment is low."
items.pourquoi_faux: A boom may bring inflation, shortages and a worsening trade balance, and it prepares the ground for the downturn.
items.correction_markdown: Mention the benefits and the problems together.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the four phases of the business cycle in order, starting at the peak, and give one feature of each.
items.solution_markdown:
Award a mark for each phase in the correct order with a feature:

- **Boom (peak):** high output and low unemployment, or rising prices.
- **Recession:** falling output and rising unemployment.
- **Depression (trough):** very low output, high unemployment and low investment.
- **Recovery:** output and employment begin to rise, and replacement investment starts.

items.enonce_markdown:
In an imaginary economy a firm needs 4 units of capital for each unit of annual output (a capital-output ratio of 4). National output (in billion FCFA) is 500 in year 1, 550 in year 2, 580 in year 3 and 580 in year 4. Assume that all investment is net investment induced by the change in output.

(a) Calculate net investment in years 2, 3 and 4.
(b) Explain what the results show about the effect of slowing growth on investment.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Net investment = capital-output ratio x change in output. Year 2: 4 x (550 - 500) = **200**. Year 3: 4 x (580 - 550) = **120**. Year 4: 4 x (580 - 580) = **0** (billion FCFA).

(b) Output rises in years 2 and 3, but because growth slows, net investment **falls from 200 to 120** and then to zero when output stops growing. A fall in investment lowers aggregate demand through the multiplier and can turn a slowdown into a downturn. Award a mark for linking the fall in investment to the start of a recession.

items.enonce_markdown: Discuss to what extent a government can smooth the business cycle.
items.solution_markdown:
Award marks for the following points:

- **Knowledge:** the government can use expansionary fiscal and monetary policy in a slump (more spending, lower taxes, lower interest rates) and contractionary policy in a boom, so as to stabilise aggregate demand.
- **Analysis:** higher spending in a slump raises income through the multiplier and reduces unemployment; restraint in a boom lowers inflationary pressure.
- **Limits:** the phase of the cycle is hard to identify in time; policies work with time lags and may reinforce the next phase; expansion can increase the deficit and public debt; confidence matters, so lower interest rates may not raise investment; shocks such as a fall in world commodity prices are beyond national control; a small open economy depends strongly on its trading partners.
- **Judgement:** **a government can reduce but not eliminate fluctuations**, and success depends on timing, the size of the shock and credibility.

items_markdown: The business cycle is the irregular fluctuation of real output around its trend, in four phases: boom, recession, depression (trough) and recovery.
A recession is a fall in output (commonly two consecutive quarters); slower growth with rising output is not yet a recession.
Replacement investment late in the slump marks the turning point to recovery, and returning confidence and the multiplier amplify it.
Causes include volatile investment, the accelerator ($I_{net} = v \times \Delta Y$), expectations, credit conditions and external shocks.
Policy: expansionary in a slump and contractionary in a boom, but timing, time lags, deficits and external shocks limit its success.
